stem: A 45-year-old woman has 2 months of fatigue and shortness of breath on exertion. Respiratory rate is 22/min. Heart and lung examinations are normal. Arterial blood gas on room air: PaO2 98 mm Hg, PaCO2 40 mm Hg, O2 saturation 98%. Hemoglobin is 7.0 g/dL and the arterial oxygen content is 9.5 mL/dL (normal about 20). Carboxyhemoglobin is 1%.
oneliner: 45F + exertional dyspnea + RR 22, normal heart and lung exam + PaO2 98, SaO2 98%, PaCO2 40 + Hb 7.0, O2 content 9.5 mL/dL + COHb 1% → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **PaCO2 is normal** (40); hypoventilation raises PaCO2 and lowers PaO2
whyNot.B: **PaO2 is normal** (98); altitude lowers PaO2
whyNot.D: **PaO2 is normal** and lungs are clear; V/Q mismatch lowers PaO2
whyNot.E: **Carboxyhemoglobin is only 1%**; CO would raise it and shift the curve left

why: **Normal PaO2 and SaO2 with low Hb and low O2 content** = reduced carrying capacity from anemia. Dissolved O2 and saturation are unaffected.

stem: A 28-year-old man is seen 7 days after a motorcycle crash in which he lost about 2 liters of blood from an open femur fracture. He is no longer bleeding. Hemoglobin is 8.5 g/dL, MCV 88 fL, reticulocytes 7%, with normal bilirubin and LDH.
oneliner: 28M + 2 L blood loss from fracture 1 wk ago, no ongoing bleeding + Hb 8.5, MCV 88, retics 7% + normal bilirubin and LDH → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **No chronic illness and reticulocytes are high**; ACD has low retics
whyNot.C: **Bilirubin and LDH are normal**; hemolysis raises both
whyNot.D: **Normocytic (MCV 88) after one week**; iron stores take months to run out
whyNot.E: **Reticulocytes are high** and only red cells are affected; marrow is responding

why: **Large recent hemorrhage + normocytic anemia + high reticulocytes with no hemolysis markers** = marrow replacing lost red cells.

stem: A 29-year-old woman at 32 weeks of an uncomplicated pregnancy has no symptoms. Hemoglobin is 11.0 g/dL, MCV 89 fL, and ferritin is normal. She has had no bleeding.
oneliner: 29F + 32 wk uncomplicated pregnancy, asymptomatic + Hb 11.0, MCV 89, normal ferritin + no bleeding → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Ferritin is normal and MCV is normal**; IDA is microcytic with low ferritin
whyNot.B: **MCV is normal (89)**; folate deficiency is macrocytic
whyNot.C: **No bleeding and normal ferritin** in a healthy pregnancy
whyNot.E: **Normal MCV**; thalassemia trait is microcytic

why: **Healthy third-trimester woman + mildly low Hb with normal indices** = plasma volume rises more than red cell mass.

stem: A 24-year-old woman has 6 months of fatigue. She follows a vegetarian diet and has heavy menstrual periods. Hemoglobin is 9.1 g/dL, MCV 70 fL, and RDW is increased; the smear shows small, pale red cells.
oneliner: 24F + fatigue + vegetarian diet + heavy periods + Hb 9.1, MCV 70, high RDW, small pale cells → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **No chronic inflammatory illness**; and RDW is usually normal
whyNot.C: **High RDW and a clear blood-loss cause**; trait has a normal RDW and no bleeding
whyNot.D: **Microcytic (MCV 70)**; folate deficiency is macrocytic
whyNot.E: **No exposure history**; also shows basophilic stippling, not menstrual loss

why: **Heavy menses + low-iron diet + microcytic hypochromic cells with high RDW** = chronic blood loss exhausting iron stores.

stem: A 68-year-old man has 3 months of fatigue and looks pale. Hemoglobin is 8.4 g/dL, MCV 68 fL, white cell count normal, platelets 520,000/µL. The smear shows small, pale red cells.
oneliner: 68M + fatigue and pallor + Hb 8.4, MCV 68, platelets 520k, normal WBC + small pale red cells → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Presents in infancy** with severe anemia, not at 68 with a new anemia
whyNot.B: **Microcytic (MCV 68)**; B12 deficiency is macrocytic
whyNot.C: **Platelets are high and WBC normal**; aplastic anemia is pancytopenic
whyNot.D: **White cell count is normal**; CML has marked leukocytosis

why: **Older adult + microcytic hypochromic anemia + reactive thrombocytosis** = chronic occult GI blood loss until proven otherwise.

stem: A 58-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis for 15 years has fatigue and pallor. Her joints are mildly swollen. Hemoglobin is 10.2 g/dL and MCV is 77 fL. Serum iron is 35 µg/dL (normal 60-170) and transferrin saturation is low. A bone marrow biopsy with Prussian blue stain shows abundant iron stored in marrow macrophages, with little iron in developing red cell precursors.
oneliner: 58F + RA 15 yr + fatigue, pallor + Hb 10.2, MCV 77, low serum iron + marrow Prussian blue: iron trapped in macrophages → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Marrow iron stores are present**; IDA has absent marrow iron
whyNot.B: **Iron is low and a chronic inflammatory disease is present**; trait has normal iron studies
whyNot.D: **Iron is trapped in macrophages with a chronic inflammatory cause**; MDS shows dysplasia and usually macrocytosis
whyNot.E: **Marrow shows stored iron, not abnormal cells**; infiltration gives a leukoerythroblastic picture

answer: Anemia of chronic disease (anemia of inflammation)
why: **Chronic inflammation + low serum iron + iron trapped in marrow macrophages** = hepcidin-driven iron sequestration.

stem: A 44-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus for 12 years has fatigue. Hemoglobin is 10.4 g/dL, MCV 84 fL, reticulocytes 0.6%. Serum iron is 30 µg/dL (normal 60-170), TIBC 220 µg/dL (normal 250-400), and ferritin 410 ng/mL (normal 15-150). White cell and platelet counts are normal.
oneliner: 44F + SLE 12 yr + Hb 10.4, MCV 84, retics 0.6% + iron 30, TIBC 220, ferritin 410 → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **TIBC is low and ferritin is high**; IDA has high TIBC and low ferritin
whyNot.C: **Serum iron is low**; sideroblastic anemia has high iron and ferritin
whyNot.D: **Platelets and white cells are normal**; aplastic anemia is pancytopenic
whyNot.E: **Normocytic with low iron and high ferritin**; thalassemia has microcytosis and normal iron studies

why: **Chronic autoimmune disease + low iron, low TIBC, high ferritin + low reticulocytes** = inflammation-driven hepcidin block.

stem: A couple asks for counseling after their 2-year-old son was found to have anemia. He has hemoglobin 8.6 g/dL, MCV 58 fL, target cells on the smear, and a palpable spleen tip. His mother has mild microcytosis with normal iron studies and normal hemoglobin electrophoresis. DNA testing shows she has two alpha-globin genes deleted on the same chromosome. His father is asymptomatic and has one alpha-globin gene deleted. Both parents are of Southeast Asian descent.
oneliner: 2M + microcytic anemia (Hb 8.6, MCV 58), target cells, splenomegaly + mother 2 α-genes deleted in cis, father 1 α-gene deleted → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Both parents carry alpha-globin deletions**, not beta-globin mutations
whyNot.B: **Inherited alpha-gene deletions with normal parental iron studies** explain the microcytosis
whyNot.C: **Alpha-gene deletions**, not a beta-chain Glu6Lys substitution
whyNot.E: **Alpha-gene deletions** in both parents, not a beta-chain Glu6Val mutation

why: **Three of four alpha genes deleted (two in cis from the mother + one from the father) + microcytic anemia with splenomegaly** = HbH disease (excess beta chains form β4 tetramers).

stem: A 4-year-old girl of Cypriot descent has needed regular transfusions since infancy for severe microcytic anemia. Sequencing of her beta-globin genes shows a point mutation (A to G) at an intron-exon splice site on both alleles. Pre-mRNA processing is impaired and little functional beta-globin mRNA is made.
oneliner: 4F + transfusion-dependent microcytic anemia since infancy, Cypriot + both β-globin alleles: splice-site A→G mutation, defective mRNA processing → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Mutation is in the beta-globin gene** and is a splicing defect; alpha thal is mostly gene deletion
whyNot.C: **No Glu6Val missense change**; the defect is a splice-site mutation reducing beta chains
whyNot.D: **No Glu6Lys substitution**; the defect lowers mRNA production
whyNot.E: **Inherited beta-globin splice mutation** with transfusion dependence from infancy

why: **Splice-site mutation in the beta-globin gene = impaired mRNA processing and reduced beta chains**, the commonest mechanism of beta-thalassemia.

stem: A 5-month-old boy of Greek descent is pale and fails to thrive. Examination shows hepatosplenomegaly. Hemoglobin is 5.2 g/dL. The smear shows microcytes, target cells, and nucleated red cells. Electrophoresis shows mostly hemoglobin F, with no hemoglobin A or S.
oneliner: 5M + pallor, failure to thrive, hepatosplenomegaly, Greek + Hb 5.2, target cells, nucleated RBCs + no HbA or HbS, mostly HbF → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **No HbA with high HbF**; severe alpha loss gives Hb Barts or HbH
whyNot.B: **No sickled cells or HbS** and HbF is high with no HbA
whyNot.C: **Target cells, nucleated red cells, and HbF excess** with hepatosplenomegaly
whyNot.D: **Microcytes and target cells, not spherocytes**, and HbA is absent

why: **Severe anemia at 5 months + target cells and nucleated RBCs + no HbA, high HbF** = absent beta-chain production, with gamma chains compensating after the fetal switch.

stem: A 30-year-old Greek man has mild microcytosis (hemoglobin 12.5 g/dL, MCV 66 fL) with normal ferritin and hemoglobin A2 5.8%. DNA testing shows a heterozygous beta-zero mutation. His wife has a similar picture with a heterozygous beta-plus mutation. Their 1-year-old son inherited both mutations. He has hemoglobin 7.8 g/dL, splenomegaly, target cells on smear, HbF 60%, and some HbA.
oneliner: 1M + anemia, splenomegaly, target cells, HbF 60%, some HbA + father β0 carrier (HbA2 5.8%), mother β+ carrier → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **Parents are beta-globin carriers with raised HbA2**; alpha thal does not raise HbA2
whyNot.C: **Raised HbA2 and HbF with target cells** and normal ferritin in the parents
whyNot.D: **No HbS**; the inheritance is of two beta-thalassemia alleles
whyNot.E: **No HbC**; HbF and A2 are the elevated fractions

why: **Parents are carriers (microcytosis + high HbA2); child inherits two beta alleles with high HbF and a little HbA** = beta-thalassemia.

stem: A 41-year-old man who has worked with industrial solvents containing benzene for 15 years has weeks of fatigue, bleeding gums, and recurrent infections. His hemoglobin, white cell count, and platelet count are all low, with low reticulocytes. He has no splenomegaly or circulating blasts, and a marrow biopsy is hypocellular and replaced by fat.
oneliner: 41M + 15 yr benzene exposure + fatigue, bleeding gums, infections + pancytopenia, low retics, no blasts or splenomegaly + fatty hypocellular marrow → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **No blasts and the marrow is empty of cells**; AML has a packed marrow with blasts
whyNot.B: **Marrow is hypocellular**; MDS is usually hypercellular with dysplasia
whyNot.D: **No splenomegaly and marrow is fatty**, not fibrotic
whyNot.E: **Fat-replaced marrow after a toxin exposure with low reticulocytes**; PNH is mainly a hemolytic anemia with dark urine and thrombosis

why: **Benzene exposure + pancytopenia with low reticulocytes + hypocellular, fat-replaced marrow** = marrow failure.

stem: A 36-year-old man has had tingling and numbness in his feet and an unsteady gait for 6 months. He has followed a strict vegan diet for 12 years. Vibration and position sense are reduced in the legs and knee reflexes are brisk. Pupils react normally. Hemoglobin is 9.2 g/dL and MCV is 114 fL.
oneliner: 36M + strict vegan 12 yr + foot paresthesias, unsteady gait, ↓ vibration/position sense, brisk reflexes + normal pupils + Hb 9.2, MCV 114 → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Dorsal column and corticospinal signs**; folate deficiency gives anemia without neurologic disease
whyNot.B: **Normal pupils and macrocytic anemia**; tabes has Argyll Robertson pupils and lightning pains
whyNot.C: **Macrocytic anemia and a strict vegan diet**; MS does not cause macrocytosis
whyNot.E: **MCV is 114**; iron deficiency is microcytic and not neurologic

why: **Strict vegan + macrocytic anemia + dorsal column loss with brisk reflexes** = subacute combined degeneration from B12 deficiency.

stem: A 55-year-old woman has had fatigue for several months. She had an ileal resection for Crohn disease 8 years ago. Her mucous membranes are very pale. Hemoglobin is 8.2 g/dL and MCV is 112 fL. A peripheral blood smear is shown.
oneliner: 55F + fatigue, pale mucosa + ileal resection 8 yr ago + Hb 8.2, MCV 112 + [blood smear] → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **MCV is 112**; iron deficiency is microcytic
whyNot.C: **Folate is absorbed in the jejunum**; ileal resection removes the site of B12 absorption
whyNot.D: **Macrocytic with large oval cells**; sideroblastic anemia is usually microcytic with ring sideroblasts
whyNot.E: **Macrocytic (MCV 112)**; lead gives microcytic anemia with basophilic stippling

why: **Ileal resection (site of B12 absorption) + macrocytic anemia with macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils** = B12 deficiency.

image.prompt: Peripheral blood smear showing large oval red cells (macro-ovalocytes) and one neutrophil whose nucleus has six or more lobes, among otherwise normal-looking cells.

stem: A 62-year-old woman has had fatigue and a sore, smooth tongue for 10 months. She now has burning and tingling in both feet and cannot feel a tuning fork at the toes. She is pale. Hemoglobin is 8.0 g/dL and MCV 118 fL. The smear shows oval macrocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils. Antibodies against parietal cells and against intrinsic factor are present.
oneliner: 62F + 10 mo fatigue, glossitis, burning feet, ↓ vibration + Hb 8.0, MCV 118, hypersegmented neutrophils + anti-parietal cell and anti-intrinsic factor antibodies → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **Neuropathy and anti-intrinsic factor antibodies**; folate deficiency spares nerves
whyNot.C: **Macrocytic (MCV 118) with glossitis and neuropathy**, not microcytic
whyNot.D: **Hypersegmented neutrophils and autoantibodies against gastric cells** point to megaloblastic anemia
whyNot.E: **Parietal cell and intrinsic factor antibodies with hypersegmented neutrophils**; copper deficiency has neither

why: **Megaloblastic anemia + neuropathy + anti-parietal cell/anti-intrinsic factor antibodies** = autoimmune loss of intrinsic factor causing B12 deficiency.

stem: A 52-year-old man with chronic alcohol use and a poor diet has fatigue. There are no neurologic findings. Hemoglobin is 9.0 g/dL and MCV is 115 fL. The smear shows oval macrocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils. Red cell folate is 90 ng/mL (normal over 140), serum vitamin B12 is normal, serum homocysteine is elevated, and methylmalonic acid is normal.
oneliner: 52M + chronic alcohol use, poor diet + Hb 9.0, MCV 115, hypersegmented neutrophils + low RBC folate, normal B12 + ↑ homocysteine, normal MMA → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Methylmalonic acid is normal** and B12 is normal; B12 deficiency raises MMA
whyNot.B: **Low RBC folate with hypersegmented neutrophils** explains the anemia; liver disease alone does not raise homocysteine
whyNot.D: **Reversible nutritional pattern with low folate**; MDS has dysplasia and normal vitamin levels
whyNot.E: **Macrocytic anemia with low folate**; hemochromatosis shows iron overload

why: **Low red cell folate + high homocysteine with normal methylmalonic acid** = folate (not B12) deficiency.

stem: A 6-year-old girl is pale and mildly jaundiced. The spleen tip is palpable. Her father had a splenectomy as a child. Hemoglobin is 9.4 g/dL, MCV 82 fL, and reticulocytes 8%. The direct Coombs test is negative. A peripheral blood smear is shown.
oneliner: 6F + pallor, jaundice, splenomegaly + father splenectomized + Hb 9.4, MCV 82, retics 8%, Coombs negative + [blood smear] → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Normal MCV (82)**; beta-thalassemia is microcytic with target cells
whyNot.B: **Normal MCV**; alpha-thalassemia is microcytic with target cells
whyNot.C: **Hemolysis (jaundice, retics 8%, splenomegaly)** and normal MCV
whyNot.E: **Direct Coombs is negative** and a parent has a similar history

why: **Childhood hemolytic anemia + splenomegaly + dominant family history + negative Coombs + spherocytes on the smear** = red cell membrane (ankyrin/spectrin) defect.

image.prompt: Peripheral blood smear with many small, round, dense red cells that lack central pallor, along with a few larger polychromatic cells.

stem: A 22-year-old Black man develops fatigue, jaundice, and dark urine 2 days after starting trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for a urinary tract infection. Hemoglobin falls from 14.1 to 8.7 g/dL, indirect bilirubin is high, and the direct Coombs test is negative.
oneliner: 22M, Black + 2 d after TMP-SMX + jaundice, dark urine + Hb 14.1 → 8.7, ↑ indirect bilirubin + Coombs negative → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Direct Coombs is negative**; AIHA is Coombs positive
whyNot.C: **Coombs is negative and onset is 2 days after an oxidant sulfonamide**, not an antibody-mediated pattern
whyNot.D: **Normal Hb before the drug (14.1)**; HS is a chronic hemolytic anemia
whyNot.E: **Clear oxidant-drug trigger**; PNH hemolysis is spontaneous with morning dark urine

why: **Hemolysis and dark urine days after an oxidant sulfonamide + Black male + negative Coombs** = X-linked G6PD deficiency.

stem: A 15-year-old African American boy has had 3 self-limited episodes of dark urine and jaundice, each after taking a sulfonamide antibiotic. His brother and maternal uncle had similar episodes. His mother is healthy. His hemoglobin is normal between episodes and his spleen is not palpable.
oneliner: 15M, African American + 3 episodes dark urine/jaundice after sulfa drugs + brother and maternal uncle affected, mother healthy + normal Hb between episodes, no splenomegaly → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Episodic and normal Hb between attacks, no splenomegaly**; HS is chronic and autosomal dominant
whyNot.B: **Normal Hb between episodes and drug triggers**; sickle cell causes chronic hemolysis and pain crises
whyNot.C: **Normal Hb between episodes**; PK deficiency causes chronic hemolysis
whyNot.D: **X-linked family pattern with drug-triggered episodes**; AIHA is acquired and persistent

why: **Drug-triggered, self-limited hemolysis + affected males linked through the mother (X-linked) + normal Hb between attacks** = G6PD deficiency.

stem: A 6-month-old boy has had jaundice since the newborn period, chronic hemolytic anemia, and splenomegaly. The direct Coombs test is negative, G6PD activity is normal, osmotic fragility is normal, and there are no spherocytes on the smear. Hemoglobin electrophoresis is normal.
oneliner: 6M + jaundice since birth, chronic hemolysis, splenomegaly + Coombs negative, normal G6PD, normal osmotic fragility, no spherocytes, normal Hb electrophoresis → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **G6PD activity is normal** and hemolysis is chronic rather than episodic
whyNot.C: **No spherocytes and normal osmotic fragility**
whyNot.D: **Direct Coombs is negative** and onset is from birth
whyNot.E: **Hemoglobin electrophoresis is normal**, so there is no HbS

why: **Lifelong Coombs-negative hemolysis with normal G6PD, normal fragility, and no spherocytes** = red cell glycolysis defect; low ATP shortens red cell survival.

stem: A 3-year-old boy has had jaundice, pallor, and splenomegaly since infancy. Hemoglobin is 8.5 g/dL, reticulocytes are 9%, and the direct Coombs test is negative. Red cell enzyme studies show normal total activity of G6PD and hexokinase. For pyruvate kinase, the patient's red cells need a much higher phosphoenolpyruvate concentration to reach half the maximal velocity than normal red cells, while the maximal velocity is nearly normal.
oneliner: 3M + jaundice, splenomegaly since infancy + Hb 8.5, retics 9%, Coombs negative + normal G6PD and hexokinase, pyruvate kinase Km ↑ → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **G6PD activity is normal**; the abnormal enzyme is pyruvate kinase
whyNot.C: **An enzyme kinetic defect with chronic hemolysis**, not a membrane defect
whyNot.D: **Hexokinase activity is normal** in this patient
whyNot.E: **Direct Coombs is negative** and a specific enzyme defect is shown

why: **Increased Km of pyruvate kinase (needs more substrate) with chronic Coombs-negative hemolysis** = pyruvate kinase deficiency.

stem: A 10-month-old Black boy is irritable and has had 2 days of painful swelling of both hands and both feet. He has no fever. Hemoglobin is 7.4 g/dL and reticulocytes are 12%.
oneliner: 10M, Black + painful swollen hands and feet x 2 d, afebrile + Hb 7.4, retics 12% → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Painful hand-foot swelling (dactylitis) with brisk hemolysis**; HbC disease is mild and does not cause vaso-occlusion
whyNot.B: **Dactylitis**; beta-thal major gives severe anemia with hepatosplenomegaly, not vaso-occlusive swelling
whyNot.C: **Afebrile and symmetric** involvement of all four extremities
whyNot.E: **Dactylitis**; HS causes hemolysis but not vaso-occlusion

why: **Infant after the HbF decline + symmetric painful hand-foot swelling (dactylitis) + hemolytic anemia** = sickle cell disease.

stem: A 24-year-old Black woman has right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals. Since childhood she has had episodes of severe bone and chest pain. Ultrasound shows gallstones. Hemoglobin is 8.2 g/dL with high reticulocytes, indirect bilirubin is elevated, and AST and ALT are normal. The smear shows Howell-Jolly bodies, and the spleen is not palpable.
oneliner: 24F, Black + postprandial RUQ pain + lifelong bone and chest pain episodes + gallstones, Hb 8.2, high retics, ↑ indirect bilirubin, Howell-Jolly bodies, no palpable spleen → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **No palpable spleen and Howell-Jolly bodies** (autosplenectomy); HS has splenomegaly and no pain crises
whyNot.C: **Recurrent bone and chest pain**; G6PD hemolysis is episodic after oxidant exposure without pain crises
whyNot.D: **Pain crises with hyposplenism**; thal major has hepatosplenomegaly and transfusion dependence from infancy
whyNot.E: **Lifelong pain episodes since childhood**; AIHA is acquired and does not cause bone pain

why: **Lifelong pain crises + autosplenectomy (Howell-Jolly bodies) + chronic hemolysis with pigment gallstones** = sickle cell disease.

stem: A 26-year-old woman has had 2 weeks of fatigue and yellow eyes. She is pale and has scleral icterus. There is no family history of anemia. Hemoglobin is 7.4 g/dL, reticulocytes 10%, indirect bilirubin 3.8 mg/dL, and the direct Coombs test is positive for IgG. The smear shows small round red cells without central pallor.
oneliner: 26F + 2 wk fatigue, pallor, icterus, no family history + Hb 7.4, retics 10%, ↑ indirect bilirubin + Coombs IgG positive, spherocytes → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Retics are high with a positive Coombs**; hypersplenism gives splenomegaly and mild cytopenias
whyNot.B: **High reticulocytes and hemolysis**; ACD has a low retic count
whyNot.D: **Positive direct Coombs, acute onset, and no family history**; HS is Coombs negative
whyNot.E: **Reticulocytes 10%**; ineffective erythropoiesis has low retics and intramarrow destruction

why: **Hemolysis with reticulocytosis and indirect hyperbilirubinemia + spherocytes + positive direct Coombs (IgG)** = warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia.

stem: A 66-year-old man has had chronic lymphocytic leukemia for 8 years. He now reports 3 weeks of fatigue and yellowing of the eyes. Hemoglobin is 7.0 g/dL, reticulocytes 12%, indirect bilirubin and LDH are elevated, and haptoglobin is low. Platelet count is normal. The direct Coombs test is positive for IgG. The smear shows spherocytes and polychromatic cells.
oneliner: 66M + CLL 8 yr + 3 wk fatigue, jaundice + Hb 7.0, retics 12%, ↑ indirect bilirubin and LDH, ↓ haptoglobin + normal platelets + Coombs IgG positive, spherocytes → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Hemolysis markers and reticulocytosis**; IDA is microcytic with low retics
whyNot.B: **Reticulocytes are 12% and platelets are normal**; infiltration lowers retics and platelets
whyNot.C: **Onset at 66 with positive Coombs** in a patient with CLL
whyNot.D: **Spherocytes (no schistocytes) with normal platelets** and a positive Coombs

why: **CLL + hemolysis (retics, indirect bilirubin, low haptoglobin) + spherocytes + positive IgG Coombs** = warm AIHA complicating CLL.

stem: A 27-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of dark urine, most noticeable in the morning, along with fatigue and mild jaundice. She takes no medications. Hemoglobin is 8.1 g/dL, reticulocytes are high, LDH is elevated, and the direct Coombs test is negative.
oneliner: 27F + recurrent dark morning urine, fatigue, jaundice, no drugs + Hb 8.1, high retics, ↑ LDH, Coombs negative → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **No drug or infection trigger**; G6PD hemolysis follows oxidant stress
whyNot.C: **Episodic dark urine (intravascular hemolysis)**; HS causes chronic extravascular hemolysis with splenomegaly
whyNot.D: **Dark urine from intravascular hemolysis with high reticulocytes**; thalassemia is a microcytic anemia without hemoglobinuria
whyNot.E: **Direct Coombs is negative**

why: **Dark morning urine (hemoglobinuria) + Coombs-negative intravascular hemolysis with no trigger** = PNH: loss of GPI-anchored CD55/CD59 leaves red cells open to complement.

stem: A 58-year-old man had a mechanical aortic valve placed 5 months ago. He now has fatigue and yellow sclerae. There is an early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left sternal border. Hemoglobin is 9.0 g/dL, reticulocytes 6%, indirect bilirubin is high, LDH is high, and haptoglobin is low. Platelets are normal and the direct Coombs test is negative. AST, ALT, and alkaline phosphatase are normal. The smear shows fragmented red cells.
oneliner: 58M + mechanical aortic valve 5 mo ago + fatigue, jaundice, diastolic decrescendo murmur + Hb 9.0, retics 6%, ↑ indirect bilirubin and LDH, ↓ haptoglobin + normal platelets, Coombs negative, normal LFTs, fragmented RBCs → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.C: Hemolytic anemia from the prosthetic valve

whyNot.A: **Bilirubin is indirect and ALP is normal**; cholestasis raises direct bilirubin and ALP
whyNot.B: **AST and ALT are normal**
whyNot.D: **Direct Coombs is negative** and the smear shows fragments, not spherocytes
whyNot.E: **Platelets are normal**; TTP needs thrombocytopenia

why: **Prosthetic valve with leak + indirect hyperbilirubinemia, high LDH, low haptoglobin, fragmented red cells** = mechanical hemolysis.

stem: A 30-year-old man started dapsone 2 days ago for dermatitis herpetiformis. He now has headache and bluish lips. Oxygen saturation by pulse oximetry is 85% and does not improve with 100% oxygen. Arterial PaO2 is 98 mm Hg. Heart and lungs are normal on examination. His arterial blood is chocolate brown and stays brown on exposure to air.
oneliner: 30M + 2 d on dapsone + headache, cyanosis + SpO2 85% unchanged on 100% O2, PaO2 98 + normal heart and lungs + chocolate-brown blood → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Blood is chocolate brown and cyanosis is present**; CO gives cherry-red color and normal-looking skin
whyNot.B: **Oxidant drug trigger and brown blood**; sickle disease shows pain crises and hemolysis
whyNot.C: **Normal heart exam and normal PaO2**; shunts lower PaO2
whyNot.D: **Brown blood and cyanosis within 2 days of a new drug**; thalassemia is a chronic microcytic anemia

why: **Oxidant drug + cyanosis unresponsive to O2 with normal PaO2 + chocolate-brown blood** = iron oxidized to the ferric state, which cannot carry O2.

stem: A 2-month-old boy is fed formula mixed with water from the family's private well. He has bluish lips and skin. His heart and lungs are normal on examination, hemoglobin is normal, and the red cells look normal. His blood is chocolate brown and the cyanosis does not improve with oxygen.
oneliner: 2M + cyanosis, formula mixed with well water + normal heart and lungs, normal Hb and red cell shape + chocolate-brown blood, no response to O2 → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **Normal cardiac exam and no response to O2 with brown blood**; a shunt gives dark red blood
whyNot.C: **Hemoglobin and red cell morphology are normal**; alpha thal is microcytic
whyNot.D: **Hemoglobin is normal** and there is no jaundice or hemolysis
whyNot.E: **Normal red cell shape** and no pain or anemia

why: **Infant cyanosis with normal heart/lungs/Hb + nitrate-contaminated well water + brown blood** = nitrates oxidize Fe2+ to Fe3+.

stem: A 46-year-old man with chronic hepatitis C and heavy alcohol use has recurrent tense blisters and erosions on the backs of his hands after sun exposure. The skin is fragile, and he has facial hypertrichosis. His urine fluoresces pink-orange under a Wood lamp.
oneliner: 46M + hepatitis C, heavy alcohol + blisters on backs of hands after sun, fragile skin, facial hypertrichosis + urine fluoresces under Wood lamp → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Adult onset with blisters and urinary porphyrins**; EPP begins in childhood with burning pain and no blisters
whyNot.B: **Tense blisters with skin fragility and hypertrichosis**; pellagra gives a scaly photosensitive dermatitis (Casal necklace)
whyNot.C: **Adult onset with hepatitis C and alcohol as triggers**; XP presents in childhood with freckling and early skin cancers
whyNot.E: **Photosensitive blistering skin disease**; AIP has abdominal and neuropsychiatric attacks, no skin findings

why: **Adult with blistering on sun-exposed skin + urine fluorescence under Wood lamp + hepatitis C/alcohol** = uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency.

stem: A 66-year-old man with severe COPD has a ruddy face and chronic cough. Oxygen saturation is 87% on room air. Hemoglobin is 18.5 g/dL and hematocrit 56%. Serum erythropoietin is elevated. White cell and platelet counts are normal and the spleen is not palpable.
oneliner: 66M + severe COPD, ruddy face + SpO2 87% + Hb 18.5, Hct 56%, ↑ EPO, normal WBC and platelets, no splenomegaly → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Erythropoietin is high and SpO2 is low**; PV has low EPO, splenomegaly, and high WBC and platelets
whyNot.C: **Chronic hypoxemia and high EPO** with a true rise in red cell mass, not hemoconcentration
whyNot.D: **No splenomegaly and normal WBC and platelets**; myelofibrosis has massive splenomegaly and a leukoerythroblastic picture
whyNot.E: **Erythrocytosis**, not cytopenias, and normal other cell lines

why: **Severe COPD + hypoxemia + high EPO + erythrocytosis with normal WBC, platelets, and spleen** = hypoxia-driven erythropoietin.

stem: A 25-year-old man has a CT scan after a motor vehicle crash. The spleen is intact without laceration. At the splenic hilum there is an incidental 1.5-cm round, smooth nodule with the same enhancement as the spleen. He has no symptoms and his blood counts are normal.
oneliner: 25M + CT after car crash, intact spleen + incidental 1.5-cm smooth round nodule at splenic hilum, enhances like spleen + asymptomatic, normal counts → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **Spleen is intact with no laceration or hemoperitoneum**, and he is asymptomatic
whyNot.C: **The main spleen is in its normal position**; this is a separate small nodule
whyNot.D: **Enhances exactly like spleen**, not like a pancreatic mass
whyNot.E: **Enhancement matches splenic parenchyma** and it sits at the splenic hilum

why: **Small round nodule at the splenic hilum with spleen-like enhancement** = splenic tissue from incomplete fusion of mesenchymal buds in the dorsal mesogastrium.

stem: A 9-year-old boy has a temperature of 40.1 C, hypotension, and petechiae. Blood cultures grow Streptococcus pneumoniae. Three years ago he had abdominal surgery after a car crash and he has had no vaccines since. He has had no prior serious infections. Hemoglobin is 13 g/dL, and the smear shows Howell-Jolly bodies and target cells.
oneliner: 9M + fever 40.1, hypotension, petechiae + pneumococcal bacteremia + abdominal surgery after car crash 3 yr ago + no prior serious infections + Hb 13, Howell-Jolly bodies, target cells → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Normal hemoglobin and a history of trauma surgery**; sickle cell disease causes chronic hemolytic anemia
whyNot.B: **No prior serious infections until age 9**; Bruton disease causes recurrent infections from about 6 months
whyNot.C: **Pneumococcus, not Neisseria**, with Howell-Jolly bodies
whyNot.E: **Howell-Jolly bodies** point to absent splenic function, not antibody deficiency

why: **Prior abdominal trauma surgery + pneumococcal sepsis + Howell-Jolly bodies** = loss of splenic clearance of encapsulated bacteria.

stem: A 56-year-old man with cirrhosis from chronic hepatitis C has fatigue. Examination shows spider angiomata, ascites, and a spleen palpable 4 cm below the left costal margin. Hemoglobin is 10.8 g/dL with MCV 90 fL, white cell count 3,100/µL, and platelets 62,000/µL. Fibrinogen and D-dimer are normal. The smear shows no schistocytes. Bone marrow has normal cellularity with adequate megakaryocytes.
oneliner: 56M + cirrhosis (HCV), ascites, spleen 4 cm below costal margin + Hb 10.8, MCV 90, WBC 3,100, platelets 62k + normal fibrinogen and D-dimer, normal marrow → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Fibrinogen and D-dimer are normal** with no schistocytes
whyNot.C: **MCV is normal and all three lines are low**, with a normal marrow
whyNot.D: **Normal marrow cellularity and splenomegaly**; aplastic anemia has an empty, fatty marrow
whyNot.E: **MCV is 90**, not macrocytic, and the marrow is normal

why: **Cirrhosis with portal hypertension + splenomegaly + mild pancytopenia with normal marrow and coagulation tests** = splenic sequestration of blood cells.

stem: A 52-year-old man with myelofibrosis and massive splenomegaly falls and strikes his left flank. Blood pressure is 80/50 mm Hg and heart rate is 125/min. The left upper abdomen is tender and distended. Hematocrit falls from 34% to 24% within hours, and ultrasound shows free fluid in the peritoneal cavity.
oneliner: 52M + myelofibrosis, massive splenomegaly + left flank trauma + BP 80/50, HR 125, tender LUQ + Hct 34 → 24%, free peritoneal fluid → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Acute shock with a falling hematocrit right after trauma** to an enlarged spleen
whyNot.B: **Falling hematocrit with free fluid after left upper quadrant trauma**; perforation gives peritonitis with free air
whyNot.D: **Left upper quadrant injury with a large hematocrit drop**; bladder rupture follows pelvic trauma and causes little blood loss
whyNot.E: **Blunt trauma onset**, not pain out of proportion with an atraumatic setting

why: **Massively enlarged spleen + blunt left upper quadrant trauma + shock, falling hematocrit, and free fluid** = ruptured spleen with hemoperitoneum.

stem: A 19-year-old woman has had heavy menstrual periods since menarche at age 12, with regular 28-day cycles. She has frequent nosebleeds and bleeds for a long time after small cuts. Her father and a brother also have frequent nosebleeds. Platelet count and PT are normal, bleeding time is prolonged, and PTT is mildly prolonged.
oneliner: 19F + heavy regular periods since menarche, frequent nosebleeds, prolonged bleeding from small cuts + father and brother with nosebleeds + normal platelets and PT, ↑ bleeding time, mildly ↑ PTT → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Mucosal bleeding in a woman** with a father also affected; hemophilia is X-linked with hemarthroses
whyNot.B: **PT is normal**; afibrinogenemia prolongs PT and PTT
whyNot.C: **PT is normal** and the bleeding is lifelong
whyNot.D: **Affected father and daughter** rule out X-linked recessive inheritance

why: **Lifelong mucosal bleeding (menorrhagia, epistaxis) + autosomal dominant family history + normal platelets, long bleeding time, mildly prolonged PTT** = deficient vWF (and secondary factor VIII).

stem: A 2-year-old boy has a swollen, painful knee after a minor fall and bruises easily. Earlier he had blood in his urine. His parents are healthy, and his mother's brother had similar bleeding. Platelet count, PT, and bleeding time are normal, PTT is prolonged, and factor VIII activity is 1%.
oneliner: 2M + painful swollen knee after minor fall, easy bruising, past hematuria + maternal uncle with similar bleeding + normal platelets, PT, bleeding time, ↑ PTT + factor VIII 1% → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **Factor VIII, not factor IX, is deficient** (1%)
whyNot.C: **Bleeding time is normal** and the pattern is X-linked with joint bleeds
whyNot.D: **PT is normal**; vitamin K deficiency prolongs PT
whyNot.E: **PT is normal** and factor VIII activity is the abnormal value

why: **X-linked inheritance + hemarthrosis + isolated prolonged PTT with factor VIII 1%** = hemophilia A.

stem: An 8-year-old boy bleeds for two days after a dental extraction. He has had two prior joint bleeds, and his maternal uncle has a similar history. Platelet count, PT, and bleeding time are normal, and PTT is 80 seconds (normal 25-35). Factor VIII activity is normal. When his plasma is mixed 1:1 with plasma from a patient known to have hemophilia A, the PTT corrects to normal.
oneliner: 8M + prolonged bleeding after dental extraction, prior joint bleeds, maternal uncle affected + normal platelets, PT, bleeding time, ↑ PTT + normal factor VIII + PTT corrects when mixed with hemophilia A plasma → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Bleeding time is normal** and the inheritance is X-linked with joint bleeds
whyNot.B: **PT is normal**; factor VII deficiency prolongs PT
whyNot.C: **PT is normal**; factor V deficiency prolongs both PT and PTT
whyNot.E: **Factor VIII is normal and hemophilia A plasma corrects his PTT**, so a different intrinsic factor (IX) is missing

why: **X-linked bleeding + isolated prolonged PTT + normal factor VIII + correction when mixed with hemophilia A plasma** = factor IX deficiency.

stem: A 15-year-old girl has frequent nosebleeds, gum bleeding, and heavy menses. She takes no medications. Platelet count is 250,000/µL with normal size, PT and PTT are normal, and bleeding time is prolonged. Ristocetin-induced aggregation is normal. Aggregation is absent with ADP, collagen, and epinephrine.
oneliner: 15F + nosebleeds, gum bleeding, menorrhagia, no medications + normal platelet count and size, normal PT/PTT, ↑ bleeding time + normal ristocetin aggregation, absent ADP/collagen/epinephrine aggregation → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Ristocetin response is normal and platelets are normal in number and size**; BSS has absent ristocetin aggregation with giant platelets
whyNot.B: **Ristocetin response is normal**; vWD has abnormal ristocetin-induced aggregation
whyNot.D: **Aggregation is entirely absent with several agonists**, not a reduced secondary wave
whyNot.E: **She takes no medications**, and aspirin would not abolish aggregation with all agonists

why: **Normal platelet count + normal ristocetin response + no aggregation with ADP, collagen, epinephrine** = deficient GPIIb/IIIa.

stem: A 24-year-old woman noticed bruising and gum bleeding that began abruptly two weeks after an upper respiratory infection. There are petechiae over the feet and ankles. Platelet count is 12,000/µL, hemoglobin and white cell count are normal, and PT and PTT are normal. The smear has no schistocytes. Bone marrow shows increased megakaryocytes.
oneliner: 24F + abrupt bruising, gum bleeding 2 wk after URI + petechiae on feet and ankles + platelets 12k, normal Hb/WBC/PT/PTT, no schistocytes + marrow with ↑ megakaryocytes → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **PT and PTT are normal** with no schistocytes and no precipitating illness
whyNot.B: **Platelet count is very low**; vWD has normal platelets
whyNot.C: **Hb and WBC are normal and marrow megakaryocytes are increased**; hypersplenism needs splenomegaly and lowers several lines
whyNot.E: **Only platelets are low and megakaryocytes are increased**; aplastic marrow is empty

why: **Abrupt mucocutaneous bleeding after a viral infection + isolated thrombocytopenia with normal PT/PTT + increased marrow megakaryocytes** = antiplatelet autoantibodies with splenic destruction.

stem: A 31-year-old man with untreated HIV infection has easy bruising and scattered petechiae. Platelet count is 15,000/µL. Hemoglobin and white cell count are normal, PT and PTT are normal, and the smear shows no schistocytes. He has no fever, confusion, or kidney injury.
oneliner: 31M + untreated HIV + easy bruising, petechiae + platelets 15k, normal Hb/WBC/PT/PTT, no schistocytes + no fever, confusion, or renal injury → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Platelets are low and PTT is normal**; hemophilia has a normal platelet count and prolonged PTT
whyNot.C: **No schistocytes, fever, neurologic signs, or renal injury**
whyNot.D: **Hemoglobin and white cells are normal**
whyNot.E: **PT and PTT are normal** with no schistocytes

why: **HIV + isolated thrombocytopenia with normal PT/PTT and normal other lines** = immune thrombocytopenia.

stem: A 35-year-old woman has crops of flat, 1-mm, non-blanching red spots on her lower legs and along her waistband, and her gums bleed when she brushes. She eats a varied diet with fruit and has had no joint bleeding. PT and PTT are normal.
oneliner: 35F + flat 1-mm non-blanching spots on legs and waistband + gum bleeding + varied diet, no joint bleeds + normal PT and PTT → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **PT and PTT are normal with no joint bleeds**; hemophilia prolongs PTT and bleeds into joints
whyNot.B: **PT is normal**; vitamin K deficiency prolongs PT first
whyNot.C: **Varied diet with fruit**; scurvy gives perifollicular hemorrhages with corkscrew hairs
whyNot.D: **Spots are flat, not palpable**; IgA vasculitis gives palpable purpura

why: **Petechiae at pressure points (waistband) + gum bleeding with normal PT and PTT** = low platelets (a primary hemostasis defect).

stem: A 58-year-old man began quinine for nocturnal leg cramps 10 days ago. He now has nosebleeds, gum bleeding, and diffuse petechiae. Platelet count is 5,000/µL; hemoglobin, white cell count, PT, and PTT are normal; the smear shows no schistocytes. Platelet count rises to normal 7 days after quinine is stopped.
oneliner: 58M + quinine for leg cramps x 10 d + epistaxis, gum bleeding, petechiae + platelets 5k, normal Hb/WBC/PT/PTT, no schistocytes + platelets normalize 7 d after stopping drug → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Clear drug exposure and recovery within a week of stopping it**; ITP is not drug-related
whyNot.B: **Normal hemoglobin and no schistocytes**; TTP is a microangiopathic hemolytic anemia
whyNot.D: **PT and PTT are normal** and there are no schistocytes
whyNot.E: **Only platelets are low** and counts recover quickly after drug withdrawal

why: **New drug (quinine) + isolated severe thrombocytopenia + normal PT/PTT/Hb/WBC + recovery after withdrawal** = drug-dependent antiplatelet antibodies.

stem: A 34-year-old woman has 3 days of fever, headache, and confusion, and now passes little urine. She has had no diarrhea. She has scattered purpura. Hemoglobin is 7.6 g/dL, MCV 90 fL, platelets 18,000/µL, creatinine 2.4 mg/dL, indirect bilirubin and LDH are high, and haptoglobin is low. PT and PTT are normal and the direct Coombs test is negative. The smear shows many fragmented red cells.
oneliner: 34F + fever, confusion, oliguria, purpura, no diarrhea + Hb 7.6, platelets 18k, creatinine 2.4, ↑ LDH, ↓ haptoglobin, normal PT/PTT, Coombs negative + schistocytes → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Prominent confusion and fever with no diarrheal prodrome**; HUS is mainly renal after bloody diarrhea
whyNot.B: **PT and PTT are normal**
whyNot.C: **Hemolytic anemia with schistocytes** and renal failure
whyNot.D: **Hemolysis with schistocytes and high LDH**; aplastic anemia has low retics and an empty marrow

why: **Fever, confusion, renal failure, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with schistocytes, thrombocytopenia, normal PT/PTT** = ADAMTS13 deficiency with platelet-rich microthrombi.

stem: A 3-year-old boy had 4 days of bloody diarrhea after eating an undercooked hamburger. He is now pale with little urine output and mild edema. Blood pressure is 135/85 mm Hg. Hemoglobin is 7.2 g/dL, platelets 40,000/µL, creatinine 3.1 mg/dL, and the smear shows schistocytes. PT and PTT are normal.
oneliner: 3M + 4 d bloody diarrhea after undercooked hamburger → pallor, oliguria, edema, BP 135/85 + Hb 7.2, platelets 40k, creatinine 3.1, schistocytes, normal PT/PTT → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **Bloody diarrhea after undercooked beef in a young child** with kidney failure and no neurologic signs
whyNot.C: **Anemia with schistocytes and low platelets**; PSGN has normal platelets and no hemolysis
whyNot.D: **Bloody diarrhea, hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, and acute renal failure** are not features of rotavirus
whyNot.E: **PT and PTT are normal** with no sepsis

why: **Bloody diarrhea after undercooked hamburger (E. coli O157:H7) followed by microangiopathic hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury** = Shiga toxin-mediated HUS.

stem: A 27-year-old woman has fever of 39.5 C and hypotension two days after an unsafe termination of pregnancy. Blood oozes from her IV puncture sites and she has new petechiae. Platelets are 35,000/µL, PT 22 s, PTT 60 s, fibrinogen 90 mg/dL (normal 200-400), and D-dimer is markedly elevated. The smear shows fragmented red cells.
oneliner: 27F + septic abortion, fever 39.5, hypotension + oozing from puncture sites, petechiae + platelets 35k, ↑ PT/PTT, fibrinogen 90, ↑↑ D-dimer, fragmented RBCs → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **PT and PTT are prolonged and fibrinogen is low**; TTP has normal coagulation tests
whyNot.C: **PT, PTT, and fibrinogen are abnormal** with a septic trigger
whyNot.D: **Platelets and fibrinogen are low and D-dimer is high**; vitamin K deficiency spares both
whyNot.E: **PT and PTT prolonged with low fibrinogen and sepsis**; HUS keeps coagulation tests normal

why: **Sepsis trigger + diffuse bleeding + low platelets and fibrinogen, prolonged PT/PTT, very high D-dimer, schistocytes** = consumptive coagulopathy.

stem: A 62-year-old man is hospitalized with a deep vein thrombosis and started on unfractionated heparin. His platelet count was 250,000/µL on admission and is 44,000/µL on day 7. He has no bleeding and takes no other new drugs. Fibrinogen is normal, and his leg pain has worsened with extension of the clot.
oneliner: 62M + DVT treated with unfractionated heparin + platelets 250k → 44k on day 7 + no bleeding, normal fibrinogen, clot extension → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Fibrinogen is normal and there is no bleeding or sepsis**
whyNot.B: **Platelets fell by more than half** after heparin; AT III deficiency does not lower platelets
whyNot.C: **Platelets fell after heparin was started in an adult**; Kasabach-Merritt is platelet trapping in an infant's vascular tumor
whyNot.E: **Thrombosis rather than bleeding** and a fall 5-10 days after a heparin start

why: **Platelets fall >50% 5-10 days after heparin + thrombosis, not bleeding** = antibodies to platelet factor 4-heparin complexes causing platelet activation.

stem: A 7-year-old boy with cystic fibrosis and greasy, foul-smelling stools has frequent nosebleeds and easy bruising. There is no family history of bleeding. Platelet count and fibrinogen are normal. PT is 24 seconds (normal 11-14) and PTT is 50 seconds (normal 25-35). Albumin is normal.
oneliner: 7M + cystic fibrosis, greasy stools + nosebleeds, easy bruising, no family history + normal platelets, fibrinogen, albumin + ↑ PT and PTT → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **PT is prolonged** and there is no family history; hemophilia prolongs only PTT
whyNot.B: **PT is prolonged**; vWD has a normal PT and no malabsorption
whyNot.D: **PT and PTT are prolonged**; scurvy has normal clotting tests
whyNot.E: **Albumin is normal and fibrinogen is normal**, with fat malabsorption explaining the coagulopathy

why: **Fat malabsorption (cystic fibrosis) + mucocutaneous bleeding + prolonged PT and PTT with normal platelets and fibrinogen** = failed gamma-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX, X.

stem: A 6-day-old exclusively breastfed boy, born at home without any injection after delivery, has bleeding from the umbilical stump and black stools. He is afebrile and feeding well. Platelets are normal and PT and PTT are prolonged.
oneliner: 6-day-old M + exclusively breastfed, home birth, no injection at birth + umbilical stump bleeding, black stools + afebrile, feeding well + normal platelets, ↑ PT and PTT → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.E: Vitamin K deficiency bleeding of the newborn

whyNot.A: **PT is prolonged**; hemophilia A prolongs only PTT
whyNot.B: **Scurvy does not appear at 6 days** and clotting tests would be normal
whyNot.C: **Afebrile and feeding well**, with normal platelets
whyNot.D: **PT is prolonged and onset is in the newborn period**

answer: Vitamin K deficiency bleeding of the newborn
why: **No prophylaxis + breastfed + umbilical/GI bleeding + prolonged PT and PTT** = low stores and low milk vitamin K, so factors II, VII, IX, X are not carboxylated.

stem: A 74-year-old widower living alone eats mostly tea and toast. He has bleeding, swollen gums and large bruises on his legs. Around hair follicles on his shins are small hemorrhages with corkscrew-shaped hairs. Hemoglobin is 10.1 g/dL. Platelet count is 250,000/µL, PT 12 s, and PTT 30 s.
oneliner: 74M + lives alone, tea-and-toast diet + bleeding swollen gums, leg bruises, perifollicular hemorrhages with corkscrew hairs + Hb 10.1, normal platelets, PT, PTT → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **PT is normal** and there are perifollicular hemorrhages with gum swelling
whyNot.C: **Platelet count is normal**
whyNot.D: **Corkscrew hairs and perifollicular bleeding** with swollen gums; folate deficiency gives glossitis and macrocytosis
whyNot.E: **New bruising late in life with a poor diet**; EDS is lifelong with hypermobile joints and stretchy skin

why: **Poor diet without fruit and vegetables + gingival bleeding + perifollicular hemorrhages with corkscrew hairs + normal platelets and clotting tests** = impaired collagen hydroxylation.

stem: A 48-year-old man has sudden pleuritic chest pain and shortness of breath 10 days after a long-haul flight. Heart rate is 112/min and oxygen saturation is 90% on room air. His left calf is swollen and tender. Lungs are clear to auscultation and the ECG shows sinus tachycardia.
oneliner: 48M + sudden pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea 10 d after long flight + HR 112, SpO2 90%, swollen tender left calf + clear lungs, sinus tachycardia → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **No fever or crackles; lungs are clear**, and the calf is swollen
whyNot.C: **Breath sounds are normal on both sides**, and the calf is swollen
whyNot.D: **Pleuritic pain with only sinus tachycardia on ECG**, plus a swollen calf
whyNot.E: **Pleuritic pain with hypoxemia after travel and a swollen calf**; dissection gives tearing pain radiating to the back

why: **Long-haul travel + sudden pleuritic pain, dyspnea, tachycardia, hypoxemia + swollen tender calf** = pulmonary embolism from a leg DVT.

stem: A 72-year-old woman had hip fracture surgery 6 days ago and has been in bed most of the time. She now has pain, warmth, and swelling of the left calf, which is 3 cm larger in circumference than the right. She is afebrile and the skin is not red. She has no chest pain or shortness of breath. D-dimer is elevated.
oneliner: 72F + hip fracture surgery 6 d ago, mostly bed-bound + painful, warm, swollen left calf (+3 cm) + afebrile, no skin redness, no chest symptoms + ↑ D-dimer → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **No chest pain or dyspnea**; the findings are in the leg
whyNot.B: **Afebrile with no skin redness**, and swelling follows surgery and immobility
whyNot.D: **Clear provoking factors (surgery, immobility)** at age 72 without prior clots
whyNot.E: **Provoked by surgery and immobility**, with no personal or family clotting history

why: **Recent orthopedic surgery + immobility + unilateral warm, swollen calf + high D-dimer** = DVT from Virchow triad (stasis, endothelial injury, hypercoagulability).

stem: A 26-year-old man has had 3 days of pain and swelling of the right thigh. There was no trauma, surgery, travel, or illness. His father had a clot in a leg vein at age 30. Duplex ultrasound shows thrombus in the superficial femoral vein. Protein C activity is low, while protein S activity, antithrombin activity, and tests for factor V Leiden and the prothrombin gene mutation are normal.
oneliner: 26M + unprovoked thigh swelling x 3 d, father with DVT at 30 + duplex: femoral vein thrombus + low protein C activity; normal protein S, antithrombin, factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Factor V Leiden test is normal**
whyNot.B: **Antithrombin activity is normal**
whyNot.C: **Protein S activity is normal**
whyNot.E: **Prothrombin gene testing is normal**

why: **Unprovoked young-adult DVT with family history + low protein C activity** = failure to inactivate factors Va and VIIIa.

stem: A 66-year-old man who smokes has had 3 weeks of a swollen, painful left calf. Over the past 6 months he has had back pain and has lost 10 kg. Tender cords appeared in his arm veins, resolved, and then recurred in other places. He has had no recent surgery, immobilization, or travel. Duplex shows a left popliteal vein thrombus. aPTT is normal, urinalysis is normal, and albumin is normal.
oneliner: 66M, smoker + DVT without provoking factor + 6 mo back pain, 10 kg weight loss + migratory tender venous cords + normal aPTT, urinalysis, albumin → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **New thrombosis at 66 with weight loss and back pain** and migratory thrombophlebitis, not lifelong clotting history
whyNot.B: **aPTT is normal**, and weight loss with migratory thrombophlebitis points to cancer
whyNot.C: **Urinalysis and albumin are normal**
whyNot.D: **First clot at 66 with weight loss and migratory thrombophlebitis**; inherited deficiency presents young

why: **Unprovoked DVT + migratory superficial thrombophlebitis + weight loss and back pain in a smoker** = occult cancer causing a hypercoagulable state.

stem: A 40-year-old man receiving a red cell transfusion develops fever, flank pain, and chest tightness 15 minutes into the infusion. His blood pressure falls to 80/50 mm Hg, and his urine turns red. His plasma is pink.
oneliner: 40M + 15 min into RBC transfusion + fever, flank pain, chest tightness, BP 80/50 + red urine, pink plasma → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Hypotension, flank pain, and hemoglobinuria**; FNHTR is fever alone
whyNot.C: **Fever, flank pain, and red urine (hemolysis)**; anaphylaxis gives urticaria, wheeze, and angioedema without hemolysis
whyNot.D: **Pink plasma and red urine** show hemolysis, with flank pain starting minutes into the transfusion
whyNot.E: **Red urine and pink plasma show hemolysis**; TRALI causes hypoxemia with bilateral lung infiltrates

why: **Symptoms minutes into a transfusion + fever, flank pain, hypotension, hemoglobinuria** = ABO-mismatched antibody-complement lysis (type II hypersensitivity).

stem: A 58-year-old woman received 3 units of red cells for a GI bleed 9 days ago and had a normal course until now. She has new fatigue and mild jaundice. Hemoglobin has fallen from 10.5 to 7.5 g/dL, reticulocytes are up, indirect bilirubin is up, and the direct Coombs test is positive. A new anti-Kidd antibody is identified in her serum. She has no fever or signs of infection and she was pregnant twice in the past.
oneliner: 58F + transfusion 9 d ago, then fatigue, jaundice + Hb 10.5 → 7.5, ↑ retics, ↑ indirect bilirubin + Coombs positive, new anti-Kidd antibody + prior pregnancies → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **A new alloantibody (anti-Kidd) appeared 9 days after transfusion** with prior sensitizing pregnancies
whyNot.B: **Onset is 9 days later**, not during or within hours of the transfusion
whyNot.C: **Hemolysis began only after transfusion, at age 58**; HS is lifelong
whyNot.E: **No fever or infection**

why: **Prior sensitization (pregnancies) + hemolysis days to weeks after transfusion + new Kidd alloantibody** = anamnestic response against minor red cell antigens.

stem: A 55-year-old man received two units of fresh frozen plasma after surgery for a coagulopathy. Three hours later he has acute dyspnea, fever, and oxygen saturation of 84% on 4 L/min. Blood pressure is 95/55 mm Hg. There are bilateral crackles but his jugular veins are flat. BNP is normal. Chest x-ray shows new bilateral infiltrates, and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure is 10 mm Hg.
oneliner: 55M + 2 units FFP 3 h ago + dyspnea, fever, SpO2 84%, BP 95/55, bilateral crackles, flat neck veins + normal BNP, bilateral infiltrates, wedge 10 → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.D: Acute respiratory distress syndrome from sepsis

whyNot.A: **Flat neck veins, normal BNP, low wedge pressure, and low BP**; TACO has hypertension, JVD, and high BNP
whyNot.B: **Fever with bilateral infiltrates**; anaphylaxis gives urticaria, wheeze, and angioedema

stem: A 12-hour-old boy is jaundiced. His mother is a 32-year-old woman who is Rh-negative; her first pregnancy ended in a miscarriage at 10 weeks and she did not receive Rh immune globulin. The baby is Rh-positive. His hemoglobin is 11 g/dL, bilirubin is 11 mg/dL (mostly indirect), reticulocytes are high, and the direct Coombs test is positive.
oneliner: 12-h M + jaundice + Rh-negative mother with prior miscarriage, no RhIG; baby Rh-positive + Hb 11, indirect bilirubin 11, high retics, Coombs positive → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Mother is Rh-negative with an Rh-positive baby and prior sensitizing pregnancy**; no ABO mismatch is described
whyNot.B: **Hemoglobin is low-normal with hemolysis**; polycythemia gives a high hematocrit
whyNot.C: **Anemia with hemolysis and a positive Coombs**; FAIT is isolated low platelets
whyNot.D: **Jaundice in the first 24 hours with hemolysis and a positive Coombs**; physiologic jaundice starts after day 2

why: **Rh-negative mother with a prior sensitizing event + Rh-positive baby + jaundice in the first day with positive Coombs** = maternal anti-D IgG crossing the placenta.

stem: A 28-year-old Rh-negative woman delivers a stillborn Rh-positive fetus at 34 weeks. The fetus has generalized edema, ascites, and an enlarged liver and spleen, and the smear shows many nucleated red cells. Maternal anti-D antibodies are present.
oneliner: 28F, Rh-negative + stillbirth at 34 wk, Rh-positive fetus + generalized edema, ascites, hepatosplenomegaly, many nucleated RBCs + maternal anti-D antibodies → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **Maternal anti-D antibodies in an Rh-negative mother**; ABO disease is mild and rarely hydropic
whyNot.C: **Maternal anti-D with an Rh-positive fetus** explains the hydrops
whyNot.D: **Anti-D antibodies and many nucleated red cells** point to immune hemolysis
whyNot.E: **Anti-D antibodies in an Rh-negative mother**

answer: Hemolytic disease of the newborn (erythroblastosis fetalis, hydrops fetalis)
why: **Rh-negative mother with anti-D + Rh-positive fetus + hydrops, hepatosplenomegaly, and erythroblasts** = severe Rh alloimmune hemolysis.

stem: A 5-month-old boy has had three skin abscesses and an episode of otitis media since birth, and now has gingivitis. Growth is normal. White cell count is 4,800/µL with an absolute neutrophil count of 120/µL (normal over 1,000). Lymphocyte count, hemoglobin, and platelets are normal, and T-cell, B-cell, and immunoglobulin levels are normal. Marrow shows myeloid maturation arrest at the promyelocyte stage.
oneliner: 5M + skin abscesses, otitis media, gingivitis since birth + ANC 120, normal lymphocytes, Hb, platelets, normal T/B cells and immunoglobulins + marrow maturation arrest at promyelocyte stage → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **T, B, and immunoglobulin levels are normal** and lymphocyte count is normal; SCID has lymphopenia and opportunistic infections
whyNot.B: **T-cell count is normal**; the defect is isolated neutropenia
whyNot.C: **Growth is normal and only neutrophils are low**; congenital CMV gives growth restriction, microcephaly, and hepatosplenomegaly
whyNot.E: **Neutrophil count is very low**; CGD has normal neutrophil numbers with defective killing

why: **Recurrent bacterial infections from early infancy + very low ANC with normal other lines and immunity + promyelocyte maturation arrest** = severe congenital neutropenia.

stem: A 67-year-old man has 4 days of fever and productive cough. Chest x-ray shows a right lower lobe consolidation, and sputum Gram stain shows gram-positive diplococci. White cell count is 62,000/µL, hemoglobin and platelets are normal, and the spleen is not palpable. A peripheral blood smear is shown.
oneliner: 67M + fever, productive cough, RLL consolidation, gram-positive diplococci + WBC 62k, normal Hb and platelets, no splenomegaly + [blood smear] → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **The smear shows mature left-shifted neutrophils, not blasts**, and Hb and platelets are normal
whyNot.C: **Older adult with pneumonia and a neutrophil-predominant smear**, not lymphoblasts
whyNot.D: **Toxic granulation and Döhle bodies with an obvious infection, no basophilia or splenomegaly**; CML has basophilia, splenomegaly, and low LAP
whyNot.E: **Neutrophilic leukocytosis with a bacterial infection**, not mature small lymphocytes

why: **Severe infection (pneumococcal pneumonia) + WBC >50,000 of left-shifted neutrophils with toxic granulation and Döhle bodies, no blasts** = reactive leukocytosis (high LAP, BCR-ABL negative), not leukemia.

image.prompt: Peripheral blood smear dominated by neutrophils, many band forms and a few metamyelocytes, with coarse dark toxic granulation and pale blue Dohle bodies in the cytoplasm; no blast cells.

stem: A 16-year-old boy has had 3 weeks of cough, dyspnea, and facial swelling. Chest x-ray shows a large anterior mediastinal mass. White cell count is 85,000/µL with circulating blasts, hemoglobin 8.5 g/dL, and platelets 40,000/µL. Flow cytometry of the blasts is positive for TdT, cytoplasmic CD3, CD7, and CD1a, and negative for surface immunoglobulin and myeloperoxidase.
oneliner: 16M + cough, dyspnea, facial swelling, anterior mediastinal mass + WBC 85k with blasts, Hb 8.5, platelets 40k + TdT+, cytoplasmic CD3+, CD7+, CD1a+, MPO negative → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Blasts are CD3+/CD7+/CD1a+ with a mediastinal mass**, not CD19+/CD10+
whyNot.B: **Blasts are MPO negative and TdT-positive** with T-cell markers
whyNot.D: **Immature TdT+ blasts, not mature CD5+/CD23+ B cells**, in a teenager
whyNot.E: **Circulating blasts with cytopenias and TdT+ T-lineage markers**, not Reed-Sternberg cells

why: **Teen with an anterior mediastinal mass + blasts that are TdT+, CD3+, CD7+, CD1a+** = T-ALL, a cancer of immature thymic T cells.

stem: A 45-year-old man has had fever and sore throat for a week. His gums are swollen and bleed easily. White cell count is 70,000/µL, hemoglobin 8 g/dL, and platelets 25,000/µL. The smear shows many blasts, some containing rod-shaped cytoplasmic inclusions that stain with myeloperoxidase. The monospot test is negative.
oneliner: 45M + 1 wk fever, sore throat + swollen bleeding gums + WBC 70k, Hb 8, platelets 25k + blasts with MPO+ rod-shaped inclusions + monospot negative → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Blasts are MPO-positive with rod-shaped inclusions**, not lymphoblasts
whyNot.B: **Blasts with anemia and thrombocytopenia and a negative monospot**; mono shows reactive lymphocytes
whyNot.C: **Blasts, anemia, and thrombocytopenia in an acute illness**; CLL has mature small lymphocytes
whyNot.D: **Blasts with cytopenias**; leukemoid reaction shows mature left-shifted neutrophils

why: **Fever, gum hypertrophy and bleeding, anemia, thrombocytopenia, and blasts with Auer rods** = AML with marrow failure.

stem: A 62-year-old woman was treated with cyclophosphamide and doxorubicin for breast cancer 7 years ago. She now has fatigue and easy bruising. Hemoglobin is 7.9 g/dL, platelets 30,000/µL, and white cell count 12,000/µL with 35% myeloperoxidase-positive blasts. Cytogenetics show loss of chromosome 7. She has no lymphadenopathy or fever.
oneliner: 62F + cyclophosphamide/doxorubicin for breast cancer 7 yr ago + fatigue, bruising + Hb 7.9, platelets 30k, 35% MPO+ blasts, monosomy 7 + no lymphadenopathy → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **No lymphadenopathy, B symptoms, or Reed-Sternberg cells**, and her prior cancer was breast
whyNot.C: **Blasts are MPO-positive** with loss of chromosome 7, a myeloid change after alkylating therapy
whyNot.D: **Cytopenias with 35% blasts**, not lymphocytosis with mature cells
whyNot.E: **Monosomy 7, not t(9;22), and a blast-predominant picture**

why: **Alkylating chemotherapy years earlier + MPO-positive blasts with chromosome 7 loss and cytopenias** = therapy-related AML.

stem: A 55-year-old man has cleaned machine parts with a benzene-containing solvent for 20 years. He has 3 weeks of fatigue, weight loss, and enlarged cervical lymph nodes. White cell count is 48,000/µL, hemoglobin 9 g/dL, and platelets 60,000/µL. About 30% of circulating cells are large pleomorphic blasts, several with Auer rods.
oneliner: 55M + 20 yr benzene solvent exposure + fatigue, weight loss, cervical nodes + WBC 48k, Hb 9, platelets 60k + 30% pleomorphic blasts with Auer rods → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Auer rods mark myeloblasts**; lymphoblasts lack them
whyNot.B: **30% blasts with Auer rods**, not a left-shifted mature granulocyte picture
whyNot.C: **Circulating blasts with cytopenias and Auer rods**
whyNot.E: **Blasts with Auer rods, anemia, and thrombocytopenia**; mono shows atypical lymphocytes

why: **Chronic benzene exposure + circulating blasts with Auer rods + anemia and thrombocytopenia** = AML.

stem: A 38-year-old woman has 1 week of gum bleeding, widespread bruises, and heavy vaginal bleeding. Hemoglobin is 8.2 g/dL, platelets 20,000/µL, PT 18 s, PTT 45 s, fibrinogen 80 mg/dL, and D-dimer is markedly elevated. Bone marrow shows 80% abnormal promyelocytes with heavy granules and bundles of rod-shaped inclusions.
oneliner: 38F + gum bleeding, bruising, vaginal bleeding + Hb 8.2, platelets 20k, ↑ PT/PTT, fibrinogen 80, ↑ D-dimer + marrow 80% granulated promyelocytes with bundles of Auer rods → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Heavily granulated promyelocytes with DIC**, not lymphoblasts
whyNot.C: **Marrow is 80% abnormal promyelocytes with DIC**, not a full range of maturing granulocytes
whyNot.D: **Abnormal promyelocytes with DIC**; monocytic leukemia has monoblasts and gum infiltration
whyNot.E: **80% abnormal promyelocytes**, far above the under 20% blasts of MDS

why: **Bleeding with DIC (low fibrinogen, high D-dimer) + marrow full of heavily granulated promyelocytes with Auer rod bundles** = APL (t(15;17) PML-RARA).

stem: A 46-year-old man has fatigue, low-grade fever, and easy bruising. The spleen is enlarged. White cell count is 140,000/µL with neutrophils, myelocytes, metamyelocytes, and basophils, blasts 3%, and a low leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score.
oneliner: 46M + fatigue, low-grade fever, bruising, splenomegaly + WBC 140k with left shift, basophils, blasts 3%, low LAP → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Blasts are only 3% with a full range of maturing granulocytes**
whyNot.B: **Granulocyte left shift rather than mature small lymphocytes**
whyNot.D: **Very high WBC with basophilia and low LAP**; myelofibrosis has teardrop cells and a dry tap
whyNot.E: **Basophilia, splenomegaly, and low LAP**; a leukemoid reaction has high LAP

why: **Marked leukocytosis with left shift and basophilia + splenomegaly + low LAP** = CML (t(9;22) BCR-ABL).

stem: A 55-year-old man was diagnosed with chronic myeloid leukemia 4 years ago. He now has fever, bone pain, and an enlarging spleen. White cell count is 120,000/µL with 60% myeloperoxidase-positive blasts. BCR-ABL remains detectable.
oneliner: 55M + CML dx 4 yr ago + fever, bone pain, enlarging spleen + WBC 120k with 60% MPO+ blasts + BCR-ABL present → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Known BCR-ABL-positive CML for 4 years** with progression, not a new leukemia
whyNot.B: **Blasts are myeloperoxidase-positive**, not lymphoid
whyNot.C: **60% blasts is above the 20% threshold**; accelerated phase has 10-19% blasts
whyNot.D: **60% blasts, fever, and bone pain** show progression beyond chronic phase

answer: Chronic myeloid leukemia in blast crisis
why: **Known CML + more than 20% blasts (60%) with constitutional symptoms and splenomegaly** = blast crisis.

stem: A 58-year-old man has left upper quadrant fullness and fatigue. The spleen is markedly enlarged and there is no lymphadenopathy. He has pancytopenia. The smear shows small lymphocytes with fine, hair-like cytoplasmic projections.
oneliner: 58M + LUQ fullness, fatigue, big spleen, no lymphadenopathy + pancytopenia + lymphocytes with hair-like projections → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Hairy projections and splenomegaly without nodes**; CLL has smudge cells and lymphadenopathy
whyNot.B: **No lymphadenopathy and hairy cytoplasmic projections**
whyNot.C: **Lymphocytes with hairy projections** rather than teardrop cells
whyNot.E: **Splenomegaly and abnormal circulating lymphocytes**; aplastic anemia has an empty marrow and no spleen enlargement

why: **Older man + massive splenomegaly without lymphadenopathy + pancytopenia + lymphocytes with hairy projections** = hairy cell leukemia (TRAP-positive B cells).

stem: A 67-year-old man has a routine CBC before cataract surgery. He feels well, with no fever, weight loss, or night sweats. Examination shows no lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly. Hemoglobin is 14.2 g/dL, platelets 210,000/µL, and absolute lymphocyte count 4,600/µL (normal 1,000-4,000). Flow cytometry shows CD5+ CD19+ CD20+ B cells with a kappa:lambda ratio of 20:1, totaling 2,100 cells/µL. CD4 and CD8 T-cell counts are normal.
oneliner: 67M + asymptomatic + ALC 4,600/µL + CD5+ kappa-restricted B cells 2,100/µL + normal T cells + no nodes or spleen → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Clonal B cells under 5,000/µL**, no cytopenias, no nodes or spleen
whyNot.B: **Kappa restriction** shows a clonal, not polyclonal, population
whyNot.D: **No lymphadenopathy**, and circulating cells are CD5+ (follicular cells are CD5-negative)
whyNot.E: **No nodes, spleen, or symptoms**, and the clone is under 5,000/µL

why: **Mild lymphocytosis with a small clonal (light-chain restricted) B-cell population under 5,000/µL** and no nodes, spleen, or cytopenias = MBL.

stem: A 58-year-old man has 3 months of headaches and itching after hot showers. He has a ruddy face and a palpable spleen tip. Oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. Hemoglobin is 20.1 g/dL, hematocrit 61%, WBC 15,000/µL, and platelets 520,000/µL. The leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score is high.
oneliner: 58M + headache + itching after hot showers + plethora + spleen tip + SpO2 97% + Hct 61% + high WBC and platelets + high LAP → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **Normal oxygen saturation**, splenomegaly, and raised WBC and platelets point to a marrow disorder
whyNot.C: **High LAP score** and erythrocytosis (CML has low LAP and no red cell excess)
whyNot.D: **Hematocrit 61%** shows red cell mass is up, not just platelets
whyNot.E: **Plethora with high hematocrit**, not anemia

why: **High Hct with plethora, splenomegaly, normal SpO2, high WBC/platelets, and high LAP** = polycythemia vera.

stem: A 49-year-old woman has 2 days of a painful, mottled blue right index finger; the radial pulse is normal. She has had easy bruising and one nosebleed this year. The spleen is not palpable. Hemoglobin is 13.2 g/dL, WBC 9,400/µL with a normal differential, and platelets 1,530,000/µL. Ferritin and CRP are normal.
oneliner: 49F + mottled blue finger with normal pulse + bruising and nosebleed + platelets 1,530,000/µL + normal Hb and WBC + normal ferritin/CRP → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Hemoglobin is normal**, no red cell excess
whyNot.B: **Normal WBC and differential**, no splenomegaly
whyNot.C: **Normal CRP and ferritin**: no inflammation or iron deficiency to explain it
whyNot.D: **No anemia and no splenomegaly**; platelets are the isolated problem

stem: A 66-year-old man has 6 months of fatigue, early satiety, and a 7-kg weight loss. The spleen is palpable 10 cm below the left costal margin. Hemoglobin is 9.1 g/dL, WBC 4,200/µL, platelets 110,000/µL, and uric acid 9.4 mg/dL. BCR-ABL1 testing is negative. A bone marrow aspiration attempt yields no marrow (dry tap).
oneliner: 66M + massive splenomegaly + weight loss + anemia + low-normal WBC + high uric acid + BCR-ABL1 negative + dry tap → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **BCR-ABL1 negative** and WBC is low-normal, not very high
whyNot.C: **Anemia**, not a high hematocrit
whyNot.D: **Platelets are low (110,000/µL)** with anemia
whyNot.E: **Massive splenomegaly and a dry tap** are not typical of MDS

why: **Massive splenomegaly, anemia, BCR-ABL1 negative, and a dry tap** = marrow fibrosis from primary myelofibrosis.

stem: A 6-year-old boy from rural Uganda has had a painless right jaw swelling that grew to 8 cm over 3 weeks. His face looks puffy and several teeth are loose. He has no fever.
oneliner: 6M + rural Uganda + jaw mass growing to 8 cm in 3 weeks + puffy face + loose teeth → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Jaw tumor growing in weeks in an endemic region**; Ewing typically arises in long bones or pelvis
whyNot.B: **Explosive growth over 3 weeks** is too fast; usually metaphysis of long bones

whyNot.E: **Endemic region, child, jaw location** fit Burkitt; DLBCL is mostly adult and sporadic

why: **Child from equatorial Africa with a rapidly growing jaw mass** = endemic Burkitt lymphoma (EBV, t(8;14)).

stem: A 15-year-old boy has a painless mass in the left posterior neck that has doubled in size over 3 weeks, with night sweats. The mass is 5 cm and firm. Excisional biopsy shows sheets of medium-sized lymphocytes with many mitoses and scattered pale macrophages containing debris. The tumor cells do not stain for keratin.

ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **Monotonous sheets of cells**, not scattered Reed-Sternberg cells in a mixed background
whyNot.D: **Solid, rapidly growing mass** with lymphoid sheets, not a cystic structure
whyNot.E: **No granulomas or necrosis**; sheets of mitotic lymphocytes

stem: A 17-year-old girl has 2 months of cough and shortness of breath when lying flat. She has firm, rubbery, nontender left cervical nodes. A chest x-ray shows a large anterior mediastinal mass. A node biopsy shows scattered large binucleate cells with owl-eye nucleoli among many small lymphocytes.
oneliner: 17F + cough and orthopnea + rubbery cervical nodes + large mediastinal mass + binucleate owl-eye cells among small lymphocytes → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **Monotonous sheets with starry-sky pattern**, not scattered large binucleate cells
whyNot.C: **Sheets of immature blasts** rather than scattered large cells in a background of mature small lymphocytes
whyNot.D: **Nodular follicles** in older adults; no owl-eye cells
whyNot.E: **Sheets of large cells**, not scattered large cells among small lymphocytes

why: **Owl-eye binucleate (Reed-Sternberg) cells among small lymphocytes with a mediastinal mass and cervical nodes** = Hodgkin lymphoma.

stem: A 61-year-old woman has had a painless, firm right neck node that has slowly enlarged over 8 months. She has no fever, weight loss, or night sweats. Excisional biopsy shows nodal architecture replaced by closely packed follicles without tingible-body macrophages. Flow cytometry shows CD19+ CD10+ B cells with a kappa:lambda ratio of 15:1.
oneliner: 61F + slow painless neck node over 8 months + packed neoplastic follicles + CD19+ CD10+ B cells + kappa restriction → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Slow growth with a follicular pattern**, not sheets of large cells
whyNot.B: **CD10-positive with follicles**; SLL is diffuse and CD5+
whyNot.C: **CD10 positivity** and neoplastic follicles; marginal zone cells are CD10-negative
whyNot.D: **Mature clonal B cells with light chain restriction**, not immature blasts in a young patient

why: **CD10+ light-chain-restricted B cells in neoplastic follicles** in an indolent node = follicular lymphoma (t(14;18)).

stem: A 57-year-old man has had itchy, scaly red patches on his trunk and buttocks for 7 years. They have not improved with topical steroids, and a KOH prep is negative. He has no history of atopy. A skin biopsy shows small clusters of atypical lymphocytes with convoluted nuclei within the epidermis.
oneliner: 57M + 7 years of itchy scaly trunk patches + steroid-resistant + KOH negative + atypical lymphocytes in epidermis → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **No atopic history** and no response to steroids; atypical epidermal lymphocytes
whyNot.C: **Patches on trunk and buttocks with atypical lymphocytes**, not silvery plaques with parakeratosis on extensors
whyNot.D: **7-year course unresponsive to steroids** with atypical lymphocytes in the epidermis on biopsy
whyNot.E: **KOH prep negative**, no response pattern of a fungal rash

stem: A 9-year-old boy had a liver transplant 8 months ago. After a rejection episode 6 weeks ago, his immunosuppression was increased. He now has 3 weeks of fever, enlarged cervical nodes, and hepatosplenomegaly. A node biopsy shows sheets of atypical B cells, and in situ hybridization for EBV is positive.
