oneliner: 9M + liver transplant + recently increased immunosuppression + fever + nodes + hepatosplenomegaly + monomorphic EBV+ B-cell sheets → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Sheets of atypical EBV+ B cells** on biopsy
whyNot.B: **Transplant recipient on intensified immunosuppression** with EBV-driven disease
whyNot.C: **Negative heterophile test** and monomorphic atypical B-cell sheets rather than reactive polyclonal lymphocytes
whyNot.E: **Lymphadenopathy with atypical B-cell sheets**, not graft lymphocytic infiltrate

why: **Increased immunosuppression after transplant plus EBV+ monomorphic B-cell proliferation** = PTLD.

stem: A 2-year-old boy has a greasy, scaly scalp rash, hepatosplenomegaly, and lytic skull lesions. Skin biopsy shows infiltrating cells that are CD1a-positive and S-100-positive.
oneliner: 2M + greasy scaly scalp rash + hepatosplenomegaly + lytic skull lesions + CD1a+ S-100+ cells on skin biopsy → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Lytic skull lesions and organomegaly** with CD1a+ cells
whyNot.B: **CD1a+ S-100+ histiocytic cells**, not leukemic blasts
whyNot.D: **2-year-old**; CD1a+ cells, not plasma cells
whyNot.E: **Toddler with organomegaly and lytic bone lesions**; CD1a+ cells, not CD4+ T cells

why: **CD1a+ S-100+ cells plus rash, organomegaly, and lytic skull lesions in a toddler** = Langerhans cell histiocytosis (Birbeck granules on EM).

stem: A 14-year-old boy has had a tender lump on his scalp for 3 weeks. A skull x-ray shows a single punched-out lytic lesion. Biopsy shows large cells with grooved nuclei and numerous eosinophils; the large cells stain positive for CD1a.
oneliner: 14M + tender scalp lump + solitary punched-out lytic skull lesion + grooved-nucleus CD1a+ cells with eosinophils → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.C: **Teenager** with grooved CD1a+ cells and eosinophils, not epithelial cells
whyNot.D: **Cellular infiltrate on biopsy**, not a fluid-filled cyst
whyNot.E: **Lesion is within the skull bone**, with CD1a+ cells, not a dural-based spindle-cell mass

stem: A 68-year-old man has had 6 weeks of worsening low back pain, fatigue, and constipation. He is tender over the lumbar vertebrae. Hemoglobin is 8.9 g/dL, serum calcium 12.4 mg/dL, creatinine 2.3 mg/dL, and total protein 10.2 g/dL with albumin 3.4 g/dL. Serum protein electrophoresis shows a large monoclonal IgG spike. oneliner: 68M + back pain + vertebral tenderness + anemia + Ca 12.4 + Cr 2.3 + high total protein with IgG spike + punched-out lytic lesions + 40% marrow plasma cells → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Normal PSA** and lytic (not blastic) lesions with a monoclonal IgG spike
whyNot.B: **Anemia, renal failure, and monoclonal spike with marrow plasma cells**; lytic punched-out lesions
whyNot.C: **IgG, not IgM, spike** with punched-out lytic bone lesions
whyNot.D: **40% marrow plasma cells** (MGUS is under 10%) with anemia, hypercalcemia, renal failure, and lytic lesions

stem: A 67-year-old man has 2 months of fatigue and bone pain. Creatinine is 4.1 mg/dL. Urine electrophoresis shows monoclonal light chains (Bence Jones protein). A kidney biopsy is shown.
oneliner: 67M + fatigue and bone pain + Cr 4.1 + Bence Jones proteinuria + [kidney biopsy photo] → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.C: **Casts of light chains with giant-cell reaction**, not sloughed epithelial cells
whyNot.D: **Bence Jones proteinuria and tubular casts**, not mesangial nodules
whyNot.E: **Bone pain with Bence Jones light chains and cast nephropathy**; no hyperviscosity picture

why: **Bence Jones proteinuria with renal failure and fractured tubular casts with giant cells** = myeloma cast nephropathy.

stem: A 71-year-old woman fractures her femur after a minor fall. X-rays show lytic lesions in the bone. A bone marrow aspirate smear is shown.

ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

stem: A 69-year-old man has routine labs before knee surgery. He feels well and has no bone pain. Serum protein electrophoresis shows a small IgG spike of 1.2 g/dL. Hemoglobin, calcium, and creatinine are normal. Urine has no light chains, and bone marrow biopsy shows 4% plasma cells. A skeletal survey is normal.
oneliner: 69M + asymptomatic + small IgG spike 1.2 g/dL + no urinary light chains + normal Hb, Ca, Cr + marrow plasma cells 4% + normal skeletal survey → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Marrow plasma cells only 4%** and no anemia, hypercalcemia, renal failure, or bone lesions
whyNot.B: **IgG, not IgM**, with no hyperviscosity or lymphoplasmacytic marrow
whyNot.D: **Monoclonal spike** rather than a polyclonal increase

stem: A 64-year-old man has 4 months of exertional dyspnea and leg swelling. Echocardiography shows thick, echo-bright ventricular walls with a small cavity and impaired filling. whyNot.C: **Light-chain plasma cell source**; no chronic inflammatory disease

oneliner: 56F + 3 weeks dyspnea + prior breast lumpectomy + nonsmoker + tamponade signs + large effusion + bloody exudate with adenocarcinoma cells → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Lifelong nonsmoker with no lung mass** on imaging
whyNot.B: **Adenocarcinoma cells** in the fluid and no fever
whyNot.D: **Malignant cells in a large bloody effusion**, not a short febrile illness
whyNot.E: **Normal creatinine**

why: **Bloody exudate with adenocarcinoma cells in a woman with prior breast cancer and no lung mass** = metastatic breast cancer to the pericardium.

stem: A 69-year-old man has 5 months of weight loss, fatigue, and iron deficiency anemia. His liver is enlarged and nodular on exam, and alkaline phosphatase is elevated. He has no history of cirrhosis, and AFP is normal. A photograph of the cut surface of the liver is shown.

whyNot.A: **Normal AFP and no cirrhosis**; multiple discrete nodules
whyNot.B: **Multiple discrete solid nodules with iron deficiency anemia** suggest spread from a bleeding GI primary, not a hemorrhagic vascular liver tumor
whyNot.C: **Older man with weight loss**, not a young woman on oral contraceptives
whyNot.D: **No cirrhosis history**, and the nodules are tumor, not regenerative

answer: Colorectal cancer metastatic to the liver
why: **Iron deficiency anemia plus multiple liver nodules without cirrhosis or high AFP** = liver metastases from a colon primary.

stem: A 70-year-old man has 3 months of changing bowel habits and blood-streaked stools. He has no fever or abdominal pain. Hemoglobin is 9.4 g/dL with a low MCV. Colonoscopy shows an ulcerated sigmoid mass, and biopsy shows invasive glandular carcinoma.

stem: A 63-year-old man has a 42 pack-year smoking history, a cough, and a 6-month weight loss. Chest x-ray shows a 4-cm central left hilar mass. Serum calcium is 13.1 mg/dL and PTH is low.
oneliner: 63M + 42 pack-years + cough + weight loss + 4-cm central hilar mass + Ca 13.1 with low PTH → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung
options.B: Small cell carcinoma of the lung
options.D: Large cell carcinoma of the lung

whyNot.D: **Central mass with PTHrP hypercalcemia**; large cell carcinoma is usually peripheral with no classic hypercalcemia
whyNot.E: **Heavy smoker with weight loss and PTHrP hypercalcemia**; carcinoid is a slow endobronchial tumor not tied to smoking

answer: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung
why: **Smoker with a central hilar mass and PTHrP-type hypercalcemia (high Ca, low PTH)** = squamous cell carcinoma of the lung.

stem: A 58-year-old man has had a 3-month weight loss and a mild cough. A chest x-ray shows multiple bilateral, well-circumscribed round nodules, mostly peripheral. There is no central mass or hilar adenopathy. Fine-needle aspiration of a nodule shows malignant epithelial cells.
oneliner: 58M + weight loss + multiple bilateral peripheral round nodules + no hilar mass + FNA malignant epithelial cells → ?

why: **Multiple bilateral peripheral well-circumscribed nodules with malignant cells and no central primary** = pulmonary metastases.

stem: A 64-year-old woman has 3 months of back pain that is worse at night and not relieved by rest. She had a mastectomy for breast cancer 6 years ago. X-rays show lytic lesions at T10 and L1. Her blood counts, creatinine, serum and urine electrophoresis are normal.

whyNot.E: **Prior breast cancer and multiple discrete lytic lesions**, not enlarged thickened bone

answer: Bone metastases (metastatic breast cancer to bone)
why: **Prior breast cancer, unremitting night pain, and multiple lytic vertebral lesions with a negative myeloma workup** = bone metastases.

stem: A 54-year-old man received standard induction chemotherapy for acute myeloid leukemia 10 days ago. He feels well and is afebrile. WBC is 600/µL with an absolute neutrophil count of 300/µL, hemoglobin 8.5 g/dL, and platelets 22,000/µL. The smear shows no blasts.

stem: A 52-year-old woman has had 6 months of progressive fatigue and shortness of breath on exertion. She is pale. She drinks no alcohol and eats a varied diet. Hemoglobin is 7.6 g/dL, white cell count 3,100/µL, platelets 92,000/µL and the reticulocyte count is low. A peripheral blood smear is shown.
